story.title: Fluent text can put the right entity in the wrong role
paragraphs: The paper gives a compact example with two facts about Williamson County: its largest city is Round Rock, and its county seat is Georgetown. A generated description instead calls Georgetown the largest city. The output uses a real entity from the input and reads naturally, but assigns that entity to the wrong relation. This is precisely the kind of mistake that a surface-level overlap score can struggle to characterize.

The example also separates two problems. The largest-city statement distorts a supplied fact, while the county-seat relation is never expressed. Fixing the wrong city removes the first error without recovering the missing information. A single quality score cannot tell a developer which repair is needed. The study therefore asks human annotators to locate errors and explain their type and severity, giving each model an interpretable error profile.

mechanism.title: Faithfulness and content selection are distinct requirements
paragraphs: The adapted MQM framework distinguishes eight error types. Inaccuracy intrinsic distorts information that is present in the source; inaccuracy extrinsic introduces information absent from it. Addition has a narrower meaning here: unnecessary or irrelevant material copied from the source. It is therefore not synonymous with hallucination. Omission, polarity errors, duplication, word form, and word order complete the taxonomy. These distinctions matter especially for ToTTo, where only highlighted table content should be described.

Annotators mark error spans and choose minor, major, or critical severity. Error penalties depend on severity and span length, normalized by output word count; omissions receive a fixed length of one. The study samples 80 inputs from each of four datasets and generates outputs from all five model configurations, producing 1,600 texts for annotation. Each text receives two independent annotations. Annotators are not told which model produced the output, reducing the influence of expectations about pre-training or model size.

evidence.title: An architectural improvement can move errors between categories
paragraphs: Copying helps preserve source content, but can also pull in content that the requested description does not need. On ToTTo, the pointer-generator lowers the omission error score from 19.74 to 7.48 relative to Transformer, while the addition score rises from 4.38 to 11.01. Those values are weighted error scores, not percentages of sentences with an error. The result explains why copying can improve overall quality while still creating a specific content-selection problem.

BLEU is not dismissed as wholly useless: its broad trend often agrees with human evaluation. But the rankings can diverge. On E2E, T5-base scores lower BLEU than T5-small, 59.96 versus 62.88, while its human score is higher, 96.36 versus 86.04. Fine-grained annotation explains what an aggregate number leaves unresolved. The interactive example lets a reader annotate the paper’s Table 2 output and score it with the same severity weights and length normalization used for the study.

reading_notes: Re-read precise MQM/PolyTope definitions, severity formula (Section 4.3, ratio 1:3:7, omission length 1), annotation protocol and Tables 2–6. Especially important: Addition means irrelevant source content, Extrinsic means unsupported content; do not conflate them. v5 demo uses the Table 2 triples and output verbatim; the paper reports types but not severities for that example.

demo.title: Annotate the output, then compare with the paper
demo.description: The study scores outputs from human error annotations: each error segment receives a type and a severity, the severity weight is multiplied by the segment length, and the total is normalized by the word count (Section 4.3). Annotate the paper’s Table 2 output yourself, then reveal the paper’s annotation.
demo.note: Adapted: input triples and output verbatim from Table 2; error types from Section 4.1; severities and the 1:3:7 ratio from Sections 4.2–4.3; omission length fixed to 1 (footnote 3). Measured: Table 6 average error scores. Computed: every score, using Equations 1–2 over this single output (20 words, punctuation not counted). The paper normalizes by all annotated outputs of a dataset (80 per model), so one output moves a system score far less. Table 2 does not report severities; its annotation is scored for every severity combination.
